cards.claim: A projectile is an object in flight after it has been thrown or projected.
cards.quote: An object that is in flight after being thrown or projected is called a projectile.

cards.claim: Projectile motion is two simultaneous independent components: horizontal motion with no acceleration and vertical motion with constant acceleration due to gravity.
cards.quote: One component is along a horizontal direction without any acceleration and the other along the vertical direction with constant acceleration due to the force of gravity.

cards.claim: The textbook's projectile model assumes air resistance has a negligible effect; drag is outside this model.
cards.quote: we shall assume that the air resistance has negligible effect on the motion of the projectile.

cards.claim: The path of a projectile (under the stated model) is a parabola.
cards.quote: This is the equation of a parabola, i.e. the path of the projectile is a parabola

cards.claim: In projectile motion the x-component of velocity stays constant and only the y-component changes, as in vertical free fall.
cards.quote: One of the components of velocity, i.e. x-component remains constant throughout the motion and only the y- component changes, like an object in free fall in vertical direction.

cards.claim: The time of flight Tf equals twice the time to reach maximum height, by the symmetry of the parabolic path.
cards.quote: Tf is known as the time of flight of the projectile. We note that Tf = 2 tm , which is expected because of the symmetry of the parabolic path.

cards.claim: For a given launch speed the horizontal range R = v0^2 sin(2 theta0)/g is maximum when sin 2theta0 is maximum, i.e. at 45 degrees (printed as 450 in the PDF text).
cards.quote: Equation (3.42a) shows that for a given projection velocity vo , R is maximum when sin 2θ0 is maximum, i.e., when θ0 = 450.

cards.claim: Ranges are equal for launch angles that exceed or fall short of 45 degrees by the same amount alpha (NCERT Example 3.6).
cards.quote: Therefore, ranges are equal for elevations which exceed or fall short of 45° by equal amounts α.

cards.claim: The level-ground time-of-flight formula does not apply when the projectile lands at a different elevation from its launch point.
cards.quote: Equation 4.24 does not apply when the projectile lands at a different elevation than it was launched

cards.claim: Maximum range at 45 degrees holds only when air resistance is neglected; with air resistance the best angle is somewhat smaller.
cards.quote: In (b), we see that the range is maximum at 45 ° . 45 ° . This is true only for conditions neglecting air resistance. If air resistance is considered, the maximum angle is somewhat smaller.

cards.claim: NCERT Example 3.8: a cricket ball thrown at 28 m/s at 30 degrees above horizontal; find maximum height, time to return to the same level, and the range.
cards.quote: A cricket ball is thrown at a speed of 28 m s–1 in a direction 30° above the horizontal. Calculate (a) the maximum height, (b) the time taken by the ball to return to the same level, and (c) the distance from the thrower to the point where the ball returns to the same level.

cards.claim: In NCERT Example 3.8 the time to return to the same level is Tf = 2 v0 sin(theta0)/g = 28/9.8 s = 2.9 s.
cards.quote: (b) The time taken to return to the same level is Tf = (2 vo sin θo )/g = (2× 28 × sin 30° )/9.8 = 28/9.8 s = 2.9 s

cards.claim: In NCERT Example 3.7 the stone hits the ground when y = -490 m; solving -490 = -(1/2)(9.8) t^2 gives t = 10 s.
cards.quote: The stone hits the ground when y(t) = – 490 m. – 490 m = –(1/2)(9.8) t2. This gives t =10 s.

cards.claim: Equal range does not mean an equal path: launches at 15 and 75 degrees give the same range but different maximum heights.
cards.quote: Note that the range is the same for initial angles of 15 ° 15 ° and 75 ° , 75 ° , although the maximum heights of those paths are different.

cards.quote: The position of a particle that is free to move can be located by two coordinates in a plane. We choose the pke of motion as the X-Y plane. We choose a suitable instant as t = O and choose the origin at the place wheret particle is situated at t = 0. Any two convenient mutually perpendicular directions in the X-Y plane are chosen the X and Y-axes.
